transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, um, thank you for seeing me. So, I guess the main reason I finally decided to make an appointment and come in is... well, it's just that I get pulled off track so, so easily. Like, it's actually getting kind of ridiculous. 

For example, just the other day I was supposed to be finishing this dashboard—it's for one of my classes, I'm working on my bachelor's right now, and it's this big project where we use Slack to communicate. Which, honestly, is a complete nightmare for me. Because I'll be staring at the screen, right? Trying to figure out the layout, and then just one single Slack ping from a classmate, or even just, like, a song lyric playing in my headphones—because I try to listen to music to help me focus, but then I'll hear a specific lyric and start thinking about the artist's whole discography—or I'll just get a completely random idea for another project that has absolutely nothing to do with what I'm supposed to be doing. 

And suddenly, I've completely lost the thread of the dashboard I was supposed to be finishing. Like, the whole mental map of what I was doing is just gone. And it's not just the dashboard, it's with everything, but that was the moment where I just sat there and realized I had spent forty-five minutes looking up something totally unrelated just because a random thought popped into my head. It's just really frustrating to constantly lose my place like that, and I feel like I'm always having to re-trace my steps just to do basic assignments, you know?
Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're sitting still?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. It's actually kind of a running joke with some of my friends, but it's honestly really embarrassing when I'm in more professional settings. Like, when we have these portfolio reviews for my major—which are already stressful enough because you're basically putting all your hard work out there to be critiqued by professors and peers—I literally cannot just sit still. 

I'll be sitting there, and I don't even realize I'm doing it at first, but my leg will just be bouncing a mile a minute. Like, my heel is just going up and down, up and down. Or I'll have a pen in my hand because I'm supposed to be taking notes on the feedback, and instead of actually writing, I'm just clicking the top of it over and over. Click, click, click. And I wear a lot of rings, usually, so if I don't have a pen, I'm twisting them around my fingers, taking them off, putting them back on, switching them to different fingers. 

And then I'm also just constantly shifting my weight in the chair, crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back. It's like my body just has all this extra energy that needs to go somewhere, even though I'm supposed to be completely focused on what the professor is saying. And the worst part is, I usually don't even notice I'm doing all of this until someone gives me a look. Like, they'll glance down at my bouncing leg, or they'll pause what they're saying because the pen clicking is getting annoying, and then I suddenly realize, 'Oh my gosh, I'm doing it again.' And I try to stop, I really do, I'll force my foot flat on the floor and put my hands in my lap, but within five minutes, without even thinking about it, I'm right back to twisting my rings or shifting around again. It's just... it's exhausting trying to keep myself still, honestly.
Do you find it hard to focus or get distracted when you're doing things you enjoy or find interesting?

You know, you would think that if it's something I actually care about or find genuinely interesting, it would be different. And I really, really want it to be different! Like, I'm super passionate about user experience design—UX design—which is a big part of what I'm studying and what I want to do after I graduate. I genuinely love it. So, I'll find this really fascinating research article about, I don't know, user interface accessibility, or I'll queue up this highly recommended, in-depth UX tutorial on YouTube that I've been genuinely excited to watch all week. 

I'll get my coffee, I'll sit down at my desk, I'm totally ready and completely interested in the topic. But then... it's like, even though I actually *want* to be learning it, my brain just sort of unplugs? I'll be sitting there, and after a few minutes, the video is still playing, or I'm scrolling down through the PDF of the article, and I suddenly kind of snap back to reality and realize my eyes have just been moving across the page, or I've been staring at the screen while the instructor is talking, and I have absolutely no idea what I just took in. 

None of it registered. It's just entirely blank. And it's so incredibly frustrating because it's not like I'm bored! I actually want to know what they're saying about wireframing or whatever, but I literally have to pause, rewind the video, or go back to the top of the page and start all over again. And sometimes I have to do that three or four times for the exact same paragraph before the words actually mean anything to me, which just makes a ten-minute tutorial take half an hour. So yeah, even with the fun stuff, or the stuff I'm genuinely invested in, the focus just kind of... evaporates, and I'm left just going through the physical motions of reading without actually reading at all.
Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?

Um, acting on impulse? Like, doing things without thinking? I don't know, I guess... not really? I mean, I don't think I'm someone who just jumps into things without any thought. Honestly, I'm usually the one who gets stuck overthinking everything, especially with my design projects. Like, I'll spend hours debating whether a button should be rounded or squared, or what hex code to use for a background color. 

So, yeah, when it comes to just doing things on a whim or making snap decisions... I can't really think of anything like that. I mean, sure, maybe I'll occasionally buy a coffee when I told myself I wouldn't, or I'll click on a YouTube video I wasn't planning to watch, but that's just normal, right? Everyone does that. It's not like I'm making huge, life-altering decisions on a whim or, I don't know, quitting a class or moving to a new city without thinking about it. 

I guess I'm trying to figure out what you mean by "acting on impulse." Like, do you mean big things, or little things? Because if you mean big things, then definitely no. I'm pretty cautious about that stuff. And even with little things, it's mostly just the distraction stuff I mentioned earlier, where my attention gets pulled away. But I wouldn't really call that an impulse, you know? It's more just my brain wandering off. So, yeah, I'd say I'm actually pretty careful about thinking things through, maybe even to a fault sometimes, especially when it comes to school and my portfolio.
Do you feel like your difficulties with focus and restlessness are affecting your relationships with friends or family?

Yeah, I mean... it definitely affects things with my friends, especially the ones I'm in the same major with. It's actually been causing a lot of tension lately, which really sucks because I absolutely hate feeling like I'm letting people down. Like, we do a lot of group projects and collaborative stuff in our design program, right? And my friends, they always tell me they love my ideas. They're always like, "Oh, your concepts are so creative," or "Your vision for this app is so innovative," and they genuinely want me in the brainstorming sessions. They love bouncing ideas off me. 

But when it comes to actually executing the work and relying on me to follow through cleanly on the timeline we set... it's a completely different story. They've started getting really hesitant to partner with me. I can just see it in their faces when the professor says we have to pick groups. They kind of avoid eye contact because they know I might miss a deadline or forget to upload my part of the project until the absolute last second, even though I'm literally sitting there stressing about it the whole time. They like my ideas, but they just can't trust my follow-through.

And it's not just school projects with friends, either. It's bled into other stuff, too. Like, over the summer, there were a couple of small freelance design contracts I managed to line up—just doing some basic landing pages and branding for a couple of local businesses. Nothing crazy, but it was really good experience and I was so proud I got them. But I ended up completely losing those contracts because I just couldn't stay on track and get the revisions back to the clients when I promised I would. I'd get distracted, or I'd be restless and couldn't sit down to finish them, and eventually the clients just moved on. 

Oh, and there was this big portfolio competition last semester that I was so, so excited about. A couple of my friends and collaborators were entering, and we were all supposed to do it together and kind of hype each other up. But I ended up missing out on it completely because I just couldn't pull my submission together in time. My friends had to just go ahead and submit their stuff without me because they couldn't wait around for me to get my act together. So, yeah, it's definitely putting a strain on things. They try to be nice about it, but I know it frustrates them, and it frustrates me too, because I know I have the talent and the ideas, it's just the actual doing-it-reliably part that messes everything up.
Have you always had difficulty with focus and restlessness, or did it start at some point in your life?

Oh, wow, um... yeah, no, it definitely didn't just start recently. It's honestly been a thing for as long as I can literally remember. Like, if you were to go back and look at my old report cards from, I don't know, second or third grade? The comments from my teachers were always exactly the same. It was like a broken record. 

They would always write these long notes to my parents about how I was just constantly rushing through my worksheets. Like, I'd just want to get them done and out of the way, so I would speed-run the math problems or the reading comprehension questions, and I'd just completely gloss over the details. And they were always saying how I was losing track of directions. The teacher would stand up at the front of the room and give us, like, three simple steps to do for an assignment, and by the time she finished, I was already doing something completely different because I just... forgot what she said or my brain just dropped the instructions entirely. Oh, and group work! I was always getting in trouble for talking over my classmates during group work. I just had so many thoughts and I couldn't hold them in, so I'd just blurt things out and interrupt people before they were even finished speaking. I didn't mean to be rude, I just couldn't wait my turn.

And then at home, it was a whole other ordeal. My parents literally had to sit right beside me at the kitchen table every single night just to get me to do my homework. It was like a hostage situation, honestly. Because if they didn't sit there and physically watch me, I would just... wander off. Like, I'd get up to get a glass of water, and then suddenly I'm in the living room playing with the dog or I'm in my bedroom trying to draw something, completely forgetting I had a spelling worksheet sitting half-finished on the table. Or I'd start one assignment, get halfway through, and then pull out a different book or start a completely different project because I got bored with the first one. So they had to hover over me constantly just to make sure I actually finished one single thing before starting another. 

So, yeah, it's definitely not a new college thing at all. It's just that now, you know, I don't have my mom sitting next to me at my desk while I try to design a wireframe or write a paper. I'm completely on my own, so the exact same stuff is happening, but the stakes are just way higher now. But yeah, the rushing, the talking over people, the wandering off... that's basically been my normal since I was a little kid.
Are there any relationships in your life, such as romantic or family relationships, that are being affected by your difficulties with focus and restlessness?

Um, wait, I feel like I kind of just... I mean, I know I just went on that whole long tangent about my friends and the people in my major, and how my group projects are basically a disaster zone right now. But as for, like, family or romantic stuff specifically? Not really. 

I mean, with my family, they already know exactly how I am. Like I was saying about them hovering over me at the kitchen table when I was a kid—they've literally seen it all. They've been dealing with it for nineteen years. Now that I'm living away at school, they aren't really in the crossfire of my day-to-day chaos anymore. Sure, sometimes my mom will text me to call her, and I'll read it, tell myself I'll call her in five minutes after I finish tweaking a font on a project, and then I completely forget for, like, three days because my brain just moves on to something else. And when I finally do call, she's definitely a little exasperated, but it's not like it's causing huge blowouts or ruining our relationship. She just kind of sighs and tells me I need to be better about checking my phone, which, fair enough. But we're good.

And then for romantic relationships... honestly, I don't even have one right now, so there's nothing to really mess up there. I can't even imagine trying to juggle a relationship on top of everything else. I'm already so stressed out just trying to keep my head above water with my classes and trying not to let my design friends down, that adding a whole other person to the mix just sounds exhausting. Like, if I had a partner, I'd probably be terrible at remembering dates or texting them back on time, but since I'm single, it's a non-issue. So, yeah, no romantic drama, and my family is pretty much just used to my scattered brain at this point. It's really just the school friends I mentioned before where it's actually causing real, tangible problems.
Are there any daily activities or tasks that you feel you're unable to complete because of your difficulties with focus and restlessness?

Um, yeah, definitely. I mean, it happens all the time with my daily coursework, which is basically my whole life right now. Like, if you want a really specific example of a task I just cannot seem to finish properly, it's whenever I get feedback on my designs. It's honestly so frustrating because I know exactly what I'm supposed to do, but I just... don't do it. 

Like, when someone—whether it's a professor or one of my group members—gives me a list of revisions to make on a project, I always start off so strong. I'll sit down at my laptop, pull up the file, and I usually do the first couple of changes right away. Like, if they say "fix the spacing on the header" or "swap out this image," I'm totally on it, boom, done. 

But then, almost immediately after I do those first two things, my brain just... derails. Instead of just going down the rest of the list and following the actual instructions, I'll start looking at the whole page and I'll just drift into redesigning something else entirely. I'll think, "Oh, what if I completely changed the shape of these buttons?" or "Let me just see what this looks like with a totally different color scheme." And I get so caught up in tweaking this new thing that nobody even asked for, mostly just because I get restless doing the boring, tedious list of corrections. 

And the worst part is, because I go off on these little tangents, I almost always leave one small but incredibly important change completely unfinished from that original list. Like, I'll completely forget to update the client's logo or fix a glaring typo that they specifically told me to fix, because I spent three hours making a new hover animation that wasn't even required. So I guess, yeah, actually finishing a set of instructions all the way through to the end without abandoning it halfway is a huge struggle for me every single day. It's like I can do the first half of a task perfectly, but actually completing it just evaporates from my mind the second I get distracted by something shinier.
Do you experience these difficulties with focus and restlessness in all settings, such as at home, in class, or while working on projects?

Um, yeah, absolutely. It's not like I can just... leave it at the door, you know? I really, really wish it worked like that. Like, if I could just say, "Okay, I'm in my dorm now, time to focus," or "I'm in class, time to sit still," but it just bleeds into literally everything I do. It honestly doesn't matter where I am. 

Like we were just talking about with the design projects, right? That's obviously a huge one, and it happens when I'm working with my groups or sitting at my laptop trying to do revisions. But even if I'm just sitting in a regular lecture hall—which is supposed to be the easiest thing in the world, right? You just sit there and listen—I just can't. I'm constantly shifting around in my seat, clicking my pen, looking at what the person three rows down is doing on their laptop, or wondering what I'm going to have for lunch, and before I know it I've completely missed what the professor was saying for the last twenty minutes. 

And then I go back to my dorm—which is basically my home right now—and it's the exact same story. I'll try to just do some basic everyday stuff, like doing my laundry or organizing my desk so I can actually have a clean space to work, and I just bounce from one thing to another. I'll put clothes in the washer, realize I need to throw away a receipt on my desk, see my sketchbook, start doodling, and then three hours later my wet clothes are just sitting there in the machine. 

It's honestly exhausting because there isn't a single place where my brain just... settles down, I guess? Whether I'm trying to listen to a lecture, or sitting at my desk trying to fix a wireframe, or even just hanging out in my room trying to fold a shirt, that restless feeling and the totally scattered focus is just always there. It's like it's attached to me. So, yeah, it really doesn't matter what setting I'm in, it just kind of follows me everywhere I go.
Are there any specific situations or activities where you feel like your difficulties with focus and restlessness are having the most significant impact on your life?

Um, yeah, definitely. I mean, it’s really hitting me the hardest professionally—or, well, pre-professionally, I guess, since I’m still in school. But in my design program, you know, you're highly encouraged to start building your network and taking on little side gigs to build your resume early on. And that is exactly where this whole... inability to just sit down and finish things cleanly is really, really costing me. 

Like, last semester, I actually managed to land a couple of small freelance contracts. Nothing crazy huge, just some branding stuff for local businesses, like this one indie coffee shop near campus that needed a new menu layout and a logo refresh. I was so excited, and my initial pitches were great! They loved the sketches. But then, when it came to actually executing the final deliverables and following through on the exact specs they asked for... I just kept getting sidetracked. I'd miss mini-deadlines because I was getting completely lost making some weird custom illustration they didn't even ask for, or I'd forget to export the files in the specific print formats they needed. And eventually, they just... pulled the contract. They literally told me they loved the art but needed someone more reliable who could just follow the brief. I ended up losing a couple of small gigs like that, and it was honestly so embarrassing.

And it’s not just the freelance stuff, either. There was this huge portfolio competition a few months ago that our department puts on every year. It’s a really big deal because actual creative directors from local agencies come to judge it, and it can totally lead to summer internships. I had all these wild, really cool concepts mapped out, and I spent weeks talking to my professors about it. But when it came down to actually compiling the pieces, formatting the presentation boards, and submitting the final polished PDF... I just couldn't pull it together. I kept tweaking tiny, irrelevant details until the very last second, got totally overwhelmed by the actual submission instructions, and literally missed the deadline. I completely missed out on the whole competition just because I couldn't follow through cleanly on the final steps. 

And honestly, the absolute worst part—and I know I kind of touched on this earlier with my major friends—is how it's affecting my reputation with the people I actually have to see every day. Like, the people in my cohort know I'm creative. They always tell me they love my ideas and my concepts when we do group brainstorming sessions. But when it comes time to actually pick partners for major collaborative projects? I can totally see them sort of... hesitating. They’ll make polite excuses or quickly pair up with someone else, because they know that if they work with me, they’re going to have to be the one to constantly manage me and make sure I’m actually doing my part of the work instead of just redesigning a single button for six hours. It really sucks, you know? Knowing they genuinely like my ideas, but they just don't want to work with me because they can't rely on me to actually get to the finish line. So, yeah, those situations are definitely where it's impacting my life the most right now.
Are your difficulties with focus and restlessness currently affecting your overall well-being or daily functioning?

Um, wow, overall well-being... I mean, I guess I haven't really stopped to think about it in those exact words? Like, I don't know if I'd say my actual well-being is, like, ruined or anything drastic like that, because, you know, I'm still hanging in there. I still have friends, even if they don't really want to do group projects with me right now, and I still really love design. Like, I genuinely love art and creating things, so it's not like I'm completely miserable or anything. 

But as far as daily functioning goes... I mean, yeah, I guess it just makes every single day feel like this massive uphill battle, which I suppose affects how I feel overall. It's just so tiring. Like, you wake up and you have this perfectly normal list of things to do—go to class, do a reading, finish a wireframe, maybe do a load of laundry—and for a normal person, that's just, you know, a regular Tuesday, right? They just do it. But for me, it's like I have to actively fight my own brain every single step of the way just to get even half of that stuff done without wandering off. 

And by the end of the day, I'm just completely drained. Not physically drained, really, because I've probably just been sitting at my desk spinning in my chair for hours or hyper-focusing on the wrong thing, but mentally, I'm just so burnt out from constantly trying to reel myself back in. I'll just be sitting there at night thinking, "Why was it so hard for me to just fold those shirts or finish that one paragraph?" 

So, I don't know if that specifically counts as affecting my well-being? I guess I just don't really have a good baseline to compare it to, because this is just how my brain has always worked. I don't really know what it feels like to just have a smooth, easy day where everything gets done. It's just... it's a lot of friction, you know? Every single day just has so much mental friction. But yeah, I don't really have a specific answer for the well-being part other than it's just really, really exhausting to constantly be managing myself all the time.
Do you feel like your difficulties with focus and restlessness are causing you significant stress or anxiety?

Um, stress or anxiety... I don't really think so? I mean, I wouldn't use those specific words for it. Like, I know people who have actual anxiety—my roommate, for example, she gets these really intense panic moments before our design critiques where she's literally shaking and worrying about every single thing that could possibly go wrong with her project, or what the professor is going to think of her. I don't get like that at all. My brain isn't really spinning with worries or, like, worst-case scenarios. It's just spinning with... well, everything else. It's more of a distracted spinning than an anxious spinning, if that makes sense? 

Like, I'm not sitting there agonizing over my future or stressing about my life choices, I'm just trying to remember where I put my drawing tablet pen while simultaneously thinking about a typography podcast I listened to three days ago. So, yeah, definitely not anxiety. 

And as for stress... I mean, sure, it's a major bummer when I miss a deadline or lose a freelance gig like I was talking about, but I don't feel this crushing, heavy stress about it. I get annoyed at myself, definitely, and it's super frustrating in the moment, but I usually just kind of bounce back and get completely absorbed in some new idea. I don't sit around chewing my nails over it for weeks. It's really just that mental friction I mentioned earlier. It's annoying, but it doesn't give me that tight feeling in my chest or keep me up at night worrying. I mean, I do stay up super late all the time, but that's usually because I'm deep down a YouTube rabbit hole about, like, mid-century modern furniture or something completely random, not because I'm stressed out. So, yeah, I really wouldn't say I'm dealing with significant stress or anxiety.
Are your difficulties with focus and restlessness making it hard for you to take care of your daily needs?

Um, no, not really. I mean, when you say "daily needs," I assume you mean like eating and sleeping and showering and all that basic human maintenance stuff, right? Because if that's what you mean, then no, I'm actually pretty okay on that front. I mean, sure, my room gets a little messy—okay, maybe a lot messy sometimes, especially right before a big critique when I have trace paper and sketches literally covering every square inch of my floor and my desk is just a mountain of empty coffee cups. But I don't ever, like, forget to eat or anything. 

Actually, I really like cooking. It's kind of a nice break from staring at screens all day. Like yesterday, for example, instead of finishing this typography assignment that I really, really needed to do, I spent two hours making this super elaborate vegetarian lasagna from scratch. I even made the ricotta from almonds because I watched this whole documentary on dairy farming last week and got super into plant-based alternatives for a minute. So I'm definitely feeding myself. If anything, I probably spend too much time on my daily needs because I use them to procrastinate on my actual work. 

And hygiene-wise, I shower every day. I actually have this whole elaborate routine with all these different scented body washes because the smells really help me wake up in the morning. I have this citrus one for when I need to feel energized, and a eucalyptus one for when I'm feeling a little overwhelmed by my to-do list. Sometimes I'll stay in the shower way too long just zoning out and thinking about color palettes or whatever, but I definitely get it done. 

Laundry is... well, laundry is annoying, and I might leave it in the basket clean for a solid week and a half before I actually fold it, but I always have clean clothes to wear. I might have to dig around in the dryer to find a matching pair of socks, but it's not like I'm walking around in dirty clothes. So I don't think my basic survival or daily needs are in jeopardy or anything. I might do them in a weird, disorganized way, or use them as an excuse to avoid my homework—like deciding I absolutely must deep-clean my entire kitchen baseboards right this second when I'm supposed to be studying—but they get done eventually. So, yeah, no, I wouldn't say it's making it hard to take care of my daily needs at all.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others or blurting out answers before they finish speaking?

Oh, wow, yeah. That is... yeah, definitely a thing I do. It's actually a huge problem, especially in my studio classes. 

Like, when we are doing group brainstorming sessions—which we do all the time in my major, right? You get together, you throw ideas at the wall, you try to figure out a direction for a project. And someone will be talking, explaining their concept for an app interface or a branding package or whatever, and they'll barely be halfway through their sentence, and my brain just instantly sees where they're going with it. Or I'll get this massive spark of inspiration based on just their first two words. And I just cannot hold it in. I'll just blurt out my idea right over them, right in the middle of their thought. 

Or, honestly, even worse than the talking is when we're working digitally. Like, if we're collaborating on a Figma board—you know Figma, right? It's this design software where you can all be in the same file and see each other's little cursors moving around in real-time. I love it, it's amazing, but it is so dangerous for me. Because someone will be verbally explaining their layout to the group, and before they've even finished explaining what they want to do, I'm already in their section of the board, dropping in shapes and changing their typography and adding my own elements to their frame. 

And I swear I'm not doing it to be mean or to take over! I'm just so genuinely excited about the direction the project is taking, and the ideas are just bubbling up so fast that they just spill out of my mouth and my hands before I can even think to put the brakes on. But then, you know, a few seconds later, the room gets kind of quiet, or I see their little cursor just stop moving on the screen, and I realize what I just did. And I can tell afterward that I totally came off as super pushy or like a massive control freak, even though I was really just hyped about the design. 

It's actually probably a huge part of why, like I mentioned earlier, people get a little weird about doing group projects with me right now. Because nobody wants to be interrupted or steamrolled while they're pitching their idea, and I completely get that! If someone did that to my work, I'd be super annoyed too. But in the moment, it just feels like this overwhelming wave of enthusiasm that I literally can't put a lid on. I just get so swept up in the creative flow that my social filter completely short-circuits. So, yeah, blurting things out and interrupting is definitely a thing that happens a lot, mostly just because I get way too excited and literally cannot wait my turn.
Do you experience difficulties with focus and restlessness during leisure activities or when doing things you enjoy?

Oh, yeah, absolutely. It’s actually kind of exhausting sometimes because even when I’m specifically trying to do something just for fun, or trying to unwind, my brain just won't let me do it quietly. 

Like, sometimes after a really intense week of studio classes, I’ll tell myself, "Okay, you need to chill. I'm just going to sit by the window and do some calm, low-stakes sketching in my sketchbook." Not for a grade, just for me, just some loose lines to relax. Or I'll try to sit down and read a book—like an actual physical fiction book, to get away from screens for a bit. 

But then I sit down, and it's just... too quiet. So I have to put on some music, right? But then the playlist isn't quite the right vibe for what I’m drawing, so I’m picking up my phone to skip tracks, and while my phone is in my hand I end up checking my notifications or looking up something totally random. And then, even if I do get back to the sketching, I start talking out loud to myself about what I'm doing. I'll be like, "Oh, this line needs to be thicker, wait, what if I made this a whole character design series?" 

And suddenly, this simple, five-minute doodle to relax turns into this massive, multi-page world-building project where I'm suddenly researching, I don't know, 19th-century botanical illustrations on my phone to get the references exactly right, and I'm narrating my whole thought process to my empty room. 

It’s the same with reading. I’ll read half a page, and the plot will give me an idea for a cool typography poster, and then I’m putting the book down and pacing around the room talking to myself about the layout. I just... I can't seem to just be quiet with it, you know? It's supposed to be this chill, peaceful leisure activity, but it always snowballs. I always end up talking to myself, or messing with my music, or checking things, or turning a tiny hobby thing into a massive project instead of just sitting there and enjoying the quiet moment. So, yeah, even my downtime ends up being pretty loud and busy.
Have you experienced difficulties with focus and restlessness consistently throughout your life?

Oh, yeah, 100 percent. It’s definitely not a new thing at all. It’s actually kind of funny—well, not funny haha, but like, my mom actually kept a bunch of my old report cards and parent-teacher conference notes in this big plastic bin in our basement. And if you go back and look at them, even way back in elementary school, it's like the exact same stuff I'm dealing with now. 

Every single year, my teachers would write these little comments in the margins about how I was rushing through my worksheets. Like, I’d just speed-run through a math or spelling worksheet because I either wanted to be the first one done, or I just wanted to flip the paper over and doodle on the back, so I'd just fly through it. And they always noted that I was constantly losing track of directions. The teacher would stand at the front of the room and be like, "Okay class, do step one, then step two, then step three," and by the time she finished talking, I was already doing step one and had completely blanked on the rest of it, so I'd have to go bother someone to ask what we were supposed to be doing. 

And the group work thing, too! They always wrote that I was talking over my classmates during group work, which makes so much sense now considering what I just told you about how I act in my college studio classes today. Even when I was like, eight years old, making a shoebox diorama or something, I was just blurting things out and steamrolling the other kids because I was so hyped up about my own vision for the project. 

And doing homework at home was honestly a whole ordeal. My parents literally used to have to pull up a chair and sit right beside me at the kitchen table every single night just to get me through it.
